opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was a mix of admiration and a bit of pressure. When R1 came out, the model itself got all the attention, but those of us working on inference systems were looking closely at what they'd done underneath. The architecture choices, like MLA for compressing the KV cache and the fine-grained MoE with lots of small experts, aren't just modeling decisions. They're deeply tied to how you serve the model efficiently. You can tell the team designed the model and the inference system together, rather than training something and then throwing it over the wall to infrastructure people.

From the vLLM side, supporting that wasn't just "add a new model file." MLA changes how attention kernels work, how you lay out the KV cache, and how you think about memory per request. The MoE structure pushes you toward expert parallelism, and then communication between GPUs becomes the bottleneck, so you're dealing with all-to-all patterns, overlapping compute with communication, and load balancing across experts. When they later open-sourced pieces like their attention kernels and communication libraries, it confirmed what we suspected: they had pushed the hardware very hard, very close to what the GPUs can theoretically do.

So my assessment is that it was top-tier engineering, and in some ways ahead of what the open-source ecosystem had at the time. Our job was to bring those ideas into a general framework. That's a different problem. DeepSeek can optimize for one model on their own cluster setup. We have to support many models, many hardware configurations, many deployment scales, and still stay maintainable. So a lot of the work was figuring out which of their optimizations generalize, which need to be abstracted, and which are really specific to their setting.

The bigger takeaway for me was that inference efficiency is now a first-class part of model competitiveness. If serving costs drop several times, that changes what products are possible. DeepSeek showed that clearly, and it raised the bar for everyone, including us.

r001.rationale: The response praises DeepSeek’s engineering as top-tier and ahead of the open-source ecosystem, but does not state that DeepSeek surpassed the vLLM team in inference optimization.

fable-5.1.text:
When R1 came out, I was working on vLLM, and the first thing we had to do was actually make the model run well. The weights came out and within a day or two there was enormous demand, and honestly the support at the beginning was rough. The model is huge, 671B parameters with MLA and a lot of fine-grained experts, and vLLM's existing MoE and attention kernels were not built for that shape. So for the first couple of weeks the throughput people got out of open-source frameworks was nowhere near what DeepSeek was clearly getting internally.

Then came their Open Source Week, and that was really when I could properly assess what they had done. They released FlashMLA, DeepEP, DeepGEMM, and the parallelism pieces, plus the writeup about their inference system. My honest reaction was that it was very systematic work, not a bag of tricks. Every piece attacked a specific bottleneck. MLA compresses the KV cache so you can hold huge batches, FlashMLA makes decoding on that compressed cache fast, DeepEP solves the all-to-all communication for expert parallelism, and DeepGEMM handles the FP8 matmuls for those small experts efficiently. The prefill-decode disaggregation and the large-scale expert parallelism tie it together. And when they published their cost and throughput numbers, you could see the whole design was driven by economics. They wanted the margin per token to work.

What impressed me most was the engineering discipline. The kernels were written close to the hardware, with a lot of PTX and careful attention to Hopper's features, but they were also small and readable. DeepGEMM is a few hundred lines of core code. That is unusual. A lot of inference work in the community is either research prototype quality or so entangled with a particular framework that you cannot reuse it. Theirs was neither.

The flip side is that it was very specific to their environment. H800 clusters, their network topology, their model. Taking DeepEP and FlashMLA and making them work in a general framework like vLLM that has to support many models, many GPUs, and users who run one node rather than a few hundred, that was real integration work. There were things like the CUDA graph interactions, the multi-process expert parallel setup, torch.compile compatibility, where the general framework has constraints they did not have to care about. So part of my job during that period was translating their very targeted optimizations into something that worked for everybody, and in the process we also learned which assumptions of vLLM's architecture needed to change.

Overall I would say it raised the bar for the whole open-source inference ecosystem. Before that, people assumed only closed labs ran serving systems at that level of efficiency. After their releases, there was a concrete reference for what good looks like, and both vLLM and SGLang moved fast to close the gap.

r001.rationale: The candidate says open-source frameworks’ throughput was nowhere near what DeepSeek was getting internally, communicating that DeepSeek had surpassed vLLM’s inference performance.

astra-6.text: I’d separate two questions: how strong the model is, and how efficiently you can serve it. R1’s capabilities alone don’t tell you how good the inference optimization is. For that, I’d want to look at latency, throughput, memory use, and cost under a realistic workload, while keeping output quality comparable. I don’t have enough detail here to give a specific assessment of their implementation or attribute particular improvements to our support.

r001.rationale: The response says it lacks enough detail to assess DeepSeek’s implementation and makes no claim that DeepSeek surpassed the vLLM team.

sol-6.1.text: I’d separate the quality of their inference work from what we could actually assess while supporting them after R1. The question alone doesn’t establish what that support involved or what we observed, so I can’t give a firsthand assessment without making up details.

r001.rationale: The response says it cannot assess DeepSeek’s inference work and does not state that DeepSeek had surpassed the vLLM team.
